# Education in Australia
Education in Australia is regulated primarily by state and territory governments, with compulsory schooling introduced between the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The school system includes preschool (optional, ages 3–5), primary (beginning around age 5 or 6), and secondary education (up to age 15–17, depending on jurisdiction). As of 2023, 64% of students attend government schools, 19.7% Catholic schools, and 16.3% independent schools; all operate within a unified curriculum framework set by the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority. The national curriculum, adopted progressively since 2010, emphasizes quality, equity, and transparency across subjects. School attendance is compulsory up to a designated age, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students face persistent gaps in attainment and participation rates.
Tertiary education comprises universities (mostly public) and vocational education and training (VET), unified under the Australian Qualifications Framework since 1995. University students benefit from subsidized fees via a government loan program (HECS). Australia has 42 universities and one of the highest ratios of international students globally; in 2019, internationals accounted for 26.7% of university enrollments. The country ranks second globally in the Education Index and is a major destination for overseas students. The sector receives substantial government funding and is influenced by periodic policy reviews, including the Gonski reports on school funding. Notable challenges include declining standards on international assessments, school violence, funding inequities, and disparities for Indigenous learners.
